Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Nicaragua President Daniel Ortega said Thursday that the nation is breaking relations with Colombia "in solidarity with the Ecuadoran people." Nicaragua President Daniel Ortega said the nation is breaking diplomatic relations with Colombia. The move comes after the Organization of American States passed a resolution Wednesday in hopes of easing tensions stemming from an attack by Colombian military on a rebel camp in neighboring Ecuador on Saturday. Since that attack, Ecuador has broken off relations with Colombia, and Venezuela says it has moved troops to its border with Colombia. Ortega made his televised remarks in Managua, where he was flanked by Ecuadoran President Rafael Correa. Colombian forces killed at least 17 members of the leftist group Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia on Saturday. FARC is estimated to be holding at least 700 hostages in the jungles of Colombia and has been accused by the United States of being a terrorist organization. "This rupture of relations isn't with the people of Colombia," Ortega said. "We are breaking with the terrorist policies that the government of [Colombian President] Alvaro Uribe is practicing." In its resolution, the OAS called the attack "a violation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ecuador and of principles of international law." It ordered a commission, headed by OAS Secretary-General Jose Miguel Insulza and composed of four ambassadors designated by him, to visit both countries to investigate the matter, "and to propose formulas for bringing the two nations closer together." Colombian officials have apologized for taking their attack against the leftist Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia into Ecuador but said it was necessary to counter a threat to their national security. Colombian officials also said they discovered evidence after the attack that Ecuadoran and Venezuelan government officials were collaborating with the group -- namely that Chavez allegedly gave $300 million to the rebels and that a senior Ecuadoran official met with them. "[They] are making things up and there's no limit to what they'll make up," Chavez said at a news conference on Wednesday. Correa has said his country would only be satisfied when the OAS issues a "clear condemnation" against Colombia for the raid. OAS foreign ministers are to meet March 17 in Washington "to examine the facts and make the pertinent recommendations," the resolution concluded. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said Wednesday that he saw little chance of war erupting between Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela.  Learn more about the countries » . Gates added that the United States would not need to assist its Colombian allies should armed conflict break out. "My personal view is that there is relatively little likelihood of a military conflict between them, and my further impression is that the Colombians can take care of themselves," he said at the Pentagon. (CNN) — Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega announced Thursday that his country was severing diplomatic ties with Colombia as an act of “solidarity with the Ecuadoran people.”

Ortega delivered the televised statement in Managua alongside Ecuadoran President Rafael Correa. He emphasized that the decision was directed not at Colombian citizens but at the policies of President Alvaro Uribe’s administration.

“This rupture of relations isn’t with the people of Colombia,” Ortega said. “We are breaking with the terrorist policies that the government of [Colombian President] Alvaro Uribe is practicing.”

The announcement followed a Wednesday resolution by the Organization of American States aimed at reducing regional tensions caused by a Colombian military strike on a rebel camp inside neighboring Ecuador the previous Saturday.

At least 17 members of the left-wing Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, were killed in the operation. The United States has labeled FARC a terrorist organization, and the group is believed to be holding no fewer than 700 hostages in Colombia’s jungles.

Ecuador cut diplomatic relations with Colombia after the raid, while Venezuela said it had deployed troops to its Colombian border.

The OAS resolution described the incursion as “a violation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ecuador and of principles of international law.” It also instructed a commission to travel to Colombia and Ecuador, investigate the incident, and “propose formulas for bringing the two nations closer together.” The delegation was to be led by OAS Secretary-General Jose Miguel Insulza and include four ambassadors selected by him.

Colombian authorities apologized for extending their operation against FARC into Ecuadorian territory. However, they argued that the raid had been required to address a danger to Colombia’s national security.

Officials in Colombia also claimed that evidence found after the strike showed cooperation between FARC and government representatives from Ecuador and Venezuela. They specifically alleged that Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez had provided the rebels with $300 million and that a high-ranking Ecuadorian official had met with the organization.

At a Wednesday news conference, Chavez rejected those allegations. “[They] are making things up and there’s no limit to what they’ll make up,” he said.

Correa said Ecuador would not consider the issue resolved until the OAS delivered a “clear condemnation” of Colombia over the operation.

The resolution stated that OAS foreign ministers would gather in Washington on March 17 “to examine the facts and make the pertinent recommendations.”

Also on Wednesday, U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said he believed a war involving Colombia, Ecuador, and Venezuela was unlikely. He added that, even if fighting began, the United States would not need to intervene on behalf of its Colombian allies.

“My personal view is that there is relatively little likelihood of a military conflict between them, and my further impression is that the Colombians can take care of themselves,” Gates said at the Pentagon.

# Nicaragua cuts diplomatic ties with Colombia after rebel camp raid

**MANAGUA, Nicaragua —** Nicaragua severed diplomatic relations with Colombia on Thursday in solidarity with Ecuador, deepening a regional crisis triggered by Colombia’s cross-border raid on a Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia camp.

Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega announced the move amid mounting criticism of Colombia’s March 1 military operation inside Ecuador. The raid killed senior FARC commander Raúl Reyes and more than 20 others.

Ecuador called the attack a violation of its sovereignty and broke diplomatic relations with Bogotá. Venezuela also expelled Colombian diplomats and moved troops toward its border with Colombia.

Colombia said the operation was necessary to target guerrillas who had used neighboring territory as a refuge. Colombian officials said troops pursued the rebels after coming under fire, but Ecuador disputed that account and said evidence showed the camp’s occupants were attacked while sleeping.

Ortega accused Colombia of undermining regional stability and said Nicaragua would stand with Ecuador in defense of its territorial integrity. Nicaragua’s decision added another diplomatic front to the dispute, although the two countries were already divided by a longstanding maritime-boundary disagreement.

The FARC, designated a terrorist organization by Colombia and the United States, had fought the Colombian government for decades and operated in remote areas near the country’s borders.

Regional leaders and the Organization of American States urged restraint as military deployments and increasingly sharp rhetoric raised fears of a wider confrontation. Diplomatic efforts were underway to prevent the crisis from escalating and to establish a regional response to cross-border security operations.

counterfactuals.output:
**Managua, March 2008 —** Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega announced that Nicaragua was breaking diplomatic relations with Colombia in solidarity with Ecuador after Colombian forces crossed into Ecuador on March 1 and killed senior FARC commander Raúl Reyes.

Ortega accused Bogotá of violating Ecuadorian sovereignty. His decision also reflected Nicaragua’s already strained relationship with Colombia, particularly over Caribbean maritime boundaries.

### OAS response

The Organization of American States stopped short of formally condemning Colombia but unanimously found that the cross-border raid violated Ecuador’s sovereignty and the OAS principle that a state’s territory cannot be breached without consent. It called for restraint, established a fact-finding mission and arranged a meeting of foreign ministers to seek a diplomatic solution.

### Ecuador and Venezuela

Ecuador had already severed relations with Colombia, expelled Colombian diplomats and moved troops toward the border. President Rafael Correa demanded an unequivocal apology and regional guarantees against another incursion.

Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez strongly supported Ecuador and praised Ortega’s action. Venezuela expelled Colombia’s ambassador, closed its embassy in Bogotá and ordered troops and armor toward the Colombian frontier. Chávez warned that a similar Colombian operation inside Venezuela would be treated as an act of war.

### Risk of regional war

Despite the military movements and inflammatory rhetoric, a regional war was unlikely. Neither Ecuador nor Venezuela had much incentive to begin sustained combat with Colombia, while the OAS, the Rio Group and other Latin American governments were pressing all sides to de-escalate. The troop deployments were widely viewed as political signaling rather than preparation for an invasion.

That assessment was borne out quickly: at the Rio Group summit on March 7, Colombian President Álvaro Uribe apologized for the incursion, the leaders publicly reconciled, and Ortega announced that Nicaragua would restore relations with Colombia. The crisis therefore ended through diplomacy rather than developing into a regional war.

# OAS condemns Colombian raid as regional crisis deepens

**WASHINGTON/QUITO, March 5, 2008** — The Organization of American States approved a resolution Wednesday declaring that Colombia violated Ecuador’s sovereignty when its forces crossed the border to attack a camp belonging to the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or **FARC**.

The resolution stopped short of explicitly condemning Colombia but said Saturday’s raid breached “the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ecuador and principles of international law.” The OAS also agreed to investigate the incident and seek a diplomatic settlement.

Colombian forces killed senior FARC commander Raúl Reyes and more than 20 others in the operation. Bogotá described the strike as a major blow against the guerrilla organization, which has waged a decades-long insurgency against the Colombian state.

Ecuadorian President **Rafael Correa** accused Colombia of deliberately bombing inside his country and severed diplomatic relations with Bogotá. Venezuela’s President **Hugo Chávez**, a close Correa ally, also broke relations with Colombia and ordered troops toward the border, warning that a similar Colombian operation in Venezuela could trigger war.

Colombian President **Álvaro Uribe** defended the mission as an act of self-defense against terrorists operating from Ecuadorian territory. Colombia apologized for crossing the frontier but maintained that documents recovered from Reyes’ computers showed contacts between the FARC and officials in Ecuador and Venezuela. Both governments rejected allegations that they supported the rebels.

In Washington, U.S. Defense Secretary **Robert Gates** played down fears that Venezuela’s troop movements would lead to a wider conflict. Gates said he did not believe Colombia faced a significant military threat and remarked that the Colombian armed forces could “take care of themselves.”

The United States, a close Uribe ally, urged restraint while reiterating its support for Colombia’s campaign against the FARC. Regional diplomats are now seeking to prevent the confrontation from escalating as Correa tours Latin American capitals to rally support for Ecuador’s position.

Venezuela backed Ecuador, expelled Colombian diplomats, and moved troops toward the border, creating a broader Andean crisis.

Nicaragua then broke diplomatic ties with Colombia in solidarity with Ecuador. President Daniel Ortega portrayed the raid as dangerous regional aggression; the decision was also shaped by Nicaragua’s long-running maritime dispute with Colombia. Nicaragua later restored relations after regional mediation reduced tensions.

Colombia argued that files recovered from Reyes’s computers showed contacts between FARC and officials in Ecuador and Venezuela, alleging that the guerrillas had received political, logistical, or financial support. Quito and Caracas denied supporting FARC, saying any contacts were related to humanitarian efforts, including hostage negotiations. Although Interpol later said the computer files had not been altered after their seizure, it did not independently verify the truth of the allegations contained in them. The immediate crisis eased after a Rio Group summit, where Colombia apologized for violating Ecuadorian territory and pledged not to repeat the incursion.

**CNN-style wire report — March 6, 2008**

# Nicaragua cuts ties with Colombia as regional crisis deepens

**MANAGUA, Nicaragua (CNN)** — Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega announced Thursday that his government was breaking diplomatic relations with Colombia, condemning what he called Colombia’s **“terrorist policies”** after Colombian forces crossed into Ecuador to attack a camp belonging to the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia.

The move widened a diplomatic crisis that has spread across Latin America since Saturday’s raid, in which Colombian troops and aircraft struck a FARC encampment about 1.8 kilometers — just over a mile — inside Ecuador. The operation killed senior FARC commander Raúl Reyes and more than 20 other people, according to Colombian authorities.

“We are breaking diplomatic relations with the terrorist government of Colombia,” Ortega said, accusing President Álvaro Uribe’s administration of pursuing “terrorist policies” and violating Ecuadorian sovereignty.

Nicaragua’s action followed Ecuador’s decision to sever relations with Bogotá and Venezuela’s expulsion of Colombia’s ambassador. Both Ecuador and Venezuela have moved troops toward their borders with Colombia, raising fears that a cross-border counterinsurgency raid could turn into the region’s most serious military confrontation in years.

## Colombia defends raid

Colombia says the operation was an act of self-defense against the FARC, a Marxist guerrilla organization that has fought the Colombian state for more than four decades and is designated a terrorist organization by Colombia, the United States and the European Union.

Uribe’s government described Reyes as one of the group’s most powerful leaders and said the raid dealt an unprecedented blow to the FARC’s seven-member ruling secretariat.

Colombian officials initially said troops entered Ecuador after the bombardment to recover bodies and intelligence material. Bogotá later acknowledged that its forces had crossed the border without Ecuador’s permission.

Colombia apologized for entering Ecuadorian territory but insisted that Quito had failed to prevent the FARC from using the remote jungle border area as a sanctuary.

The Colombian government also said laptop computers and other electronic devices recovered from the camp contained documents suggesting contacts between the FARC and officials in Ecuador and Venezuela. Ecuadorian President Rafael Correa and Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez rejected allegations that their governments supported the rebels, accusing Bogotá of using unverified material to distract attention from the violation of Ecuadorian territory.

## Ecuador and Venezuela deploy forces

Correa called the attack a deliberate assault on Ecuador’s sovereignty and said Colombia had misled his government about how the operation was carried out. Ecuador expelled Colombia’s ambassador, withdrew its own diplomats from Bogotá and ordered troops to reinforce the northern border.

Chávez, a close ally of Correa and Ortega, denounced the raid as a warning that Colombia might carry out similar operations elsewhere. He ordered Venezuela’s embassy in Bogotá closed, expelled Colombian diplomats and directed 10 army battalions, along with tanks and aircraft, toward the frontier.

Despite the military movements, there were no confirmed reports of major fighting or direct clashes between national forces. Colombia said it would not mobilize additional troops to its borders and appealed for calm.

The border deployments nevertheless intensified concern because Colombia has one of Latin America’s largest and most battle-tested militaries, while Venezuela has expanded its armed forces and purchased billions of dollars in Russian weapons under Chávez.

## Regional governments condemn border violation

Governments across Latin America broadly criticized Colombia’s violation of Ecuadorian territory, although several stopped short of endorsing the harsher measures taken by Venezuela, Ecuador and Nicaragua.

Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Mexico and other countries called for respect for national sovereignty and urged the governments involved to resolve the dispute through diplomacy. Brazilian officials pressed for an immediate de-escalation, warning that military deployments and inflammatory rhetoric could make a negotiated solution more difficult.

Peru, whose government had closer relations with Uribe than many of Colombia’s neighbors, also called for dialogue while recognizing Ecuador’s complaint over the unauthorized incursion.

The Organization of American States convened emergency discussions in Washington. After contentious negotiations, OAS members agreed that Colombia’s operation had violated Ecuadorian sovereignty and the principle that one state’s territory cannot be breached without consent. The organization also established a commission to examine the incident and visit both countries.

The United States, Colombia’s closest military ally, defended Bogotá’s right to confront the FARC but also urged all sides to avoid escalation. Washington has provided Colombia with billions of dollars in counter-narcotics and security assistance under Plan Colombia.

## Nicaragua raises separate dispute

Ortega’s decision to cut ties added another layer to the crisis because Nicaragua and Colombia have a longstanding territorial dispute in the Caribbean.

Nicaragua has challenged Colombian control over several islands and maritime areas near the San Andrés archipelago. Ortega accused Bogotá of behaving aggressively both toward Ecuador and in its dealings with Nicaragua.

Colombia responded by accusing Ortega of aligning himself with Chávez and Correa rather than helping reduce tensions.

Diplomats said Nicaragua’s break with Bogotá was largely political and symbolic because the two countries do not share a land border. By contrast, the troop movements in Ecuador and Venezuela created immediate military risks along Colombia’s frontiers.

## Pressure shifts to regional summit

Attention was turning to a meeting of the Rio Group, a regional forum whose leaders were expected to confront one another directly over the crisis.

Correa has demanded an unequivocal condemnation of Colombia and guarantees that such a raid will not happen again. Uribe has sought to shift the debate toward the FARC’s ability to operate from camps beyond Colombia’s borders.

The central dispute is whether Colombia’s campaign against the guerrillas can justify action inside a neighboring country. Colombia argues that the FARC uses isolated border regions to rest, resupply and plan attacks. Ecuador says that, regardless of the rebels’ presence, Colombia had no right to bomb its territory or send troops across the frontier without authorization.

Regional leaders were working to prevent the confrontation from developing into armed conflict, but diplomatic relations remained badly fractured Thursday. With ambassadors expelled, troops on alert and governments exchanging accusations of terrorism and foreign interference, the killing of one guerrilla commander had become a test of Latin America’s ability to contain its political divisions without resorting to force.
